title: Boston’s New Liquor Licenses Are Helping Build Third Places. Slowly.
summary: Boston’s 225 new free liquor licenses are turning bookstores and cafés into neighborhood hangouts—if they can cut through the red tape. The post Boston’s New Liquor Licenses Are Helping Build Third Places. Slowly. appeared first on Boston Magazine .
content: This story is part of a series on dining trends that appeared in the November 2026 print issue as part of the Top 50 Restaurants feature . The Little Saigon cocktail at JustBook-ish, a bookstore and gathering space in Dorchester. / Photo by Micah Fong ( @butchcamera ) When Porsha Olayiwola, Boston’s then-poet laureate , and Bing Broderick opened JustBook-ish in Fields Corner two years ago, there hadn’t been a bookstore in the neighborhood for more than three decades. There also weren’t many places where people could settle in and socialize at night. Broderick, the former executive director of the food access and housing nonprofit Haley House , says he knew what was behind the latter. “With all of the development that has happened over the last 30 years in Boston,” he says, “particularly around the Seaport and Brighton Landing, liquor licenses have been sold out from [other] communities and into those neighborhoods.” The city’s liquor license process is notoriously difficult to navigate. Unrestricted, or “value,” licenses are bought and transferred on the open market—and since Prohibition-era rules limit how many liquor licenses are in circulation, only the restaurants with the biggest budgets can shell out the hundreds of thousands of dollars required to purchase one. The process reads like a political thriller about moneyed family dynasties, out-of-state conglomerates, and private equity firms. Recently, though, that’s been changing. In late 2024, Governor Maura Healey signed a bill that established 225 new—and, more important, free—liquor licenses in Boston, with some of them earmarked for certain neighborhoods, including Dorchester. The stakes go beyond whether a restaurant can sell cocktails. In neighborhoods where liquor licenses have historically been scarce, the new licenses could make it easier for a bookstore, café, or arts space to stay open after dark—and give residents somewhere besides a traditional bar or restaurant to spend an evening. Just months after opening, JustBook-ish was awarded one of these licenses , letting it stay open at night for drinks and events. “It’s the kind of place where you meet a friend and have an after-work glass of wine,” Broderick says of the bar. “There were very few spaces for people to settle into in the evening, and our goal was to be that space.” Turkish-style eggs and labneh parfait, on the daytime café menu at Jamaica Plain’s Jadu, which turns into a wine bar at night. / Photo by Rachel Leah Blumenthal You can see the same idea taking shape elsewhere. Jadu in Jamaica Plain uses its license to operate as a café by day and wine bar by night—a “neighborhood spot always,” according to owner Maya Mukhopadhaya. Gracenote Coffee in the Leather District, meanwhile, had been relying on one-day licenses to serve wine during evening events at its Listening Room before receiving one of the new permanent licenses . For small businesses operating on thin margins and facing high rents, the ability to sell alcohol can provide an important source of revenue—and bring locals together in the process. While not as interesting as hitting up the Listening Room for a rare pressing of the Miles Electric Band, spend enough time watching videos of Boston Licensing Board meetings, and you start to hear a leitmotif. Again and again, business owners and their lawyers emphasize some version of the same thing: We want to be more than a bar or some late-night hangout. We are of this community and want to invest in it. Gracenote founder and musician Patrick Barter certainly got the sense that supporting the neighborhood mattered. “They were looking for people who had demonstrated community benefit,” he says, “and there were a lot of people [who] wrote in and supported our application in other ways, because a lot of different communities found a lot of value in what we were doing.” But Gracenote’s new license came with an unexpected hitch: The Listening Room couldn’t use it yet. To put the license to use, the takeout-only, zero-occupancy coffee operation now needs the city’s approval for a long-term change of occupancy. Then Barter will have to secure a permanent entertainment license before the Listening Room’s events can resume on a permanent basis. So he’s in a holding pattern as the required inspections and licensing process plays out. For now, the liquor license meant to help turn the Listening Room into a permanent neighborhood gathering place has instead left it silent. Barter hopes to have the room back up and running this year. It’s a fitting lesson in just how much power a liquor license can have over a third place in Boston: Getting one can help make a place possible. It just doesn’t make opening it any easier.
